- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts are rising steadily, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism, especially after recent supply auctions.
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >70), model should not overshoot by more than 2–3% in next 3–5 days; apply dampening if sentiment turns bearish or supply events increase.
- If official event net supply is negative and bearish sentiment dominates (≥0.67), model should not forecast upward trend; instead, expect mean reversion toward 68–72 range unless policy intervention.
- When sentiment is mixed (0.33–0.67) and supply events are frequent, model should not assume linear continuation; introduce volatility buffer (±1.5–2.0) around forecast mean.
- If model forecasts are rising steadily but true outcome shows early dip (e.g., 3–5 days after forecast peak), apply downward correction by 1–2% per day until sentiment stabilizes.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome deviates >5% from forecast mean, check sentiment history for 3–5 prior days: if bearish sentiment persists, reduce forecast by 1–2% per day until sentiment shifts.
- If supply events are frequent and bearish sentiment is high, model should not forecast >72 unless policy or market intervention is confirmed.
- If sentiment is bullish but true outcome is below forecast, check for supply events: if supply events are recent, reduce forecast by 1–2% per event.
- If model forecasts are flat or rising slowly but true outcome spikes, apply upward correction only if sentiment is bullish and supply events are low.
- If sentiment is bearish and true outcome is rising, reduce forecast by 1–2% per day until sentiment shifts or supply events end.
